metadata.title: Claude, Account Research.
metadata.purpose: Take the account-research skill apart in the Teardown register: explain how the SKILL.md file, trigger-phrase matching, and the three-step Read/Execute/Return pipeline actually work; name the design choice (a written spec Claude reads before acting, rather than teaching the model) and what it costs (exact-match triggers only, no graceful fallback). Lands the carry-out that account-research doesn't make Claude remember your account — it makes Claude follow the same steps to look, only when your words match what it was built to hear.
metadata.anchor_pair: B02 -> B03 ('research Acme Corp' run through the same three-step pipeline, then run again unchanged; contrasted with a non-matching request that never starts it)

beats.narration_text: Liam here, in for Bear. You ask Claude about an account, and it feels like it should already remember. It doesn't — it has to go check. So how does that checking actually work?

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'You ask about an account. Claude must already remember it, right?', hesitates on 'remember', corrects to 'check'

props.text:
You ask about an account.
Claude must already
remember it, right?

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 20-35 word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('remember' -> 'check') is visible on a late frame.

beats.narration_text: The guess is reasonable — Claude does hold enormous general knowledge. But an account's signals move today: a new hire, a funding round, a product launch. None of that lives in the corpus Claude was trained on. Here's the trade-off: pretraining optimized for scale, not for freshness. Answering from memory alone would be guessing dressed up as research.

shot.new_visual_element: A frozen 'trained on' date on a calendar; three signal cards -- new hire, funding round, product launch -- arriving after it, out of reach

production_viz.label: Nothing dated today is in memory
production_viz.mechanic: A calendar card on the left is stamped 'TRAINED ON' with a fixed date, then freezes -- no further marks land on it. To the right, three small cards draw in one at a time along a timeline running past that frozen date: 'new hire', 'funding round', 'product launch', each stamped with today's date. A dotted line from the frozen calendar toward the three cards fails to reach them and fades.

beats.narration_text: Here's the machinery. The fix is a SKILL.md file Claude reads before it acts — instructions, not memory. It only fires when your words match its triggers: 'research a company,' 'what's going on with an account,' phrases in that shape. Say 'research Acme Corp,' and it runs the same three steps every time: read the file, pull the account's signals, return them. They chose a written spec over teaching the model — the price is exact-match triggers only; the gain is that every run is identical and inspectable.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR -- 'research Acme Corp' matched against the trigger list, then walked through Read, Execute, Return

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR -- matched, then walked step by step
production_viz.mechanic: A SKILL.md card sits at top with a short list of trigger phrases beneath it: 'research [company]', 'what's going on with [company]'. THE ANCHOR. The words 'research Acme Corp' type themselves out below, a bracket snaps to the matching trigger phrase, and the query flows left to right through three labelled stations -- READ, EXECUTE, RETURN -- lighting each in turn. THIS EXACT SEQUENCE RETURNS AT B03.

beats.narration_text: Run 'research Acme Corp' again next week and Claude walks the same three steps — that's what a written spec buys you: repeatable, not remembered. But phrase it outside the trigger list, ask something the file never anticipated, and the pipeline never starts. You're back to Claude answering from what it already knows — the exact guess we started with. This works if you value repeatability; it fails the moment you need the skill to catch a question it wasn't shaped to hear.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- the same query run again, identical steps; then a non-matching question that never enters the pipeline

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- same steps again, then nothing starts
production_viz.mechanic: THE B02 SEQUENCE RETURNS, identical: 'research Acme Corp' flows through READ, EXECUTE, RETURN again, same lighted path. Beside it, a different, unmatched question types itself out, no bracket snaps to any trigger, and the three stations stay dark -- the query simply sits there, going nowhere. A line of small italic text appears beneath: 'no match. no pipeline. just Claude, on its own.'

beats.narration_text: So here's the carry-out. account-research doesn't make Claude remember your account. It makes Claude follow the same steps to look — only when your words match what it was built to hear.

props.quote: account-research doesn't make Claude remember your account. It makes Claude follow the same steps to look — only when your words match what it was built to hear.

beats.narration_text: Here's a prompt you can paste right now into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini — no account-research skill required — that runs the same three-step pipeline this whole video is about. It walks Read, Execute, Return against a company you name. Go deeper: which of the five signals gave you real information, and which just filled space?

llm_exercise.prompt: I want to run an account-research pass on a company using the same pattern the account-research skill uses. Here's my target: [paste one paragraph — the company, what you already know, and what specifically you're trying to find out]. Do this in three explicit steps, out loud, so I can see the pipeline: (1) READ — restate the trigger-shaped request in your own words and name the pattern you're matching on, so I can tell whether a real skill would have fired. (2) EXECUTE — list five specific signals worth pulling for this company (recent hires, funding, product launches, executive statements, partnerships, filings, pricing changes — pick the five that actually matter for what I asked, and say why each one matters). (3) RETURN — hand me the answer as a short brief: what changed, what it likely means, and what a follow-up query would sharpen. At the end, name one thing you'd normally have to guess at, and flag it as a guess rather than smuggling it in as fact.
llm_exercise.dig_deeper: Go deeper: which of the five signals gave you real information, and which just filled space? Rank them, and tell me what that tells you about the shape of your next query.
